kapak.alt: How to measure and interpret them

youtube.baslik: How to Measure Word Recognition Scores | Lesson 96 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
The speech discrimination score (SDS) is the percentage of words repeated correctly when they are presented at a comfortably audible level. In this lesson we cover phonetically balanced word lists, choosing the test level, recorded material versus monitored live voice (MLV), and how to interpret the scores.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology; Martin and Clark, Introduction to Audiology; Thornton and Raffin (1978), Speech-discrimination scores modeled as a binomial variable, Journal of Speech and Hearing Research.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: SDS: word lists, test level and mode of presentation
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how to measure the speech discrimination score, or SDS.
We will talk about word lists, choosing the test level, and the difference between recorded and live voice.

yan.metin: The *percentage* of words repeated correctly at a comfortable level

cumleler: The speech discrimination score, or SDS, is a suprathreshold speech test.
The SDS is the percentage of words repeated correctly when the words are presented at a comfortably audible level.
The test usually uses lists of monosyllabic words.
Today the same measure is also often called the word recognition score.
The speech recognition threshold, or SRT, shows the faintest level of recognition; the SDS, how clearly speech is understood when loud.
So the SDS tells us about the clarity dimension of a hearing loss.

yan.metin: Each word is *2 percent* in a 50-word list, 4 percent in a 25-word list

cumleler: Word lists are often phonetically balanced; they are called PB lists for short.
In a phonetically balanced list, speech sounds appear in proportions close to those of everyday language.
So the score reflects how well the overall sound structure of the language is discriminated, not just one sound.
The lists usually have twenty five or fifty words.
In a fifty-word list each word is worth two percent; in a twenty-five-word list, four percent.
There are several equivalent lists, so the same patient can be tested in both ears or at different levels.
It is also important that the words in the list are familiar words of everyday language.
Turkish also has monosyllabic word lists prepared on these principles; we will see them in the next lesson.
In the classic approach, the word list is presented thirty to forty decibels above the SRT.
This level, expressed relative to threshold, is called the sensation level, or SL.
Some clinics instead test at the most comfortable listening level, or MCL.
The aim is to get a result as close as possible to the best score the patient can achieve.
In sloping losses, a level chosen from the SRT may not make high-frequency speech sounds audible, and the score may be too low.
On the other hand, the presentation level must not exceed the uncomfortable loudness level, or UCL.
A score at a single level is not always the best score; testing at several levels is a topic we will see later.
In this example, the right ear has a sensorineural loss that slopes toward the high frequencies.
The SRT was found at thirty dB HL and agrees with the pure tone average.
By the classic rule, the word recognition test can be done at thirty plus forty, which is seventy dB HL.
At this level the low and mid frequencies are clearly audible, but speech sounds around four thousand hertz are only borderline audible.
For such a patient, an additional measurement at a higher level can prevent the score from being recorded too low.
The score must always be recorded together with the presentation level; without the level, it cannot be interpreted.
Words can be presented from recorded material or by monitored live voice, or MLV.
With recorded material, the speaker, sound quality and stress are the same in every test.
This means scores obtained at different times or in different clinics can be compared.
For this reason, most reference sources recommend recorded material for word recognition testing.
With MLV the audiologist reads the words into the microphone; it is fast and flexible for each patient.
However, the score can change with the speaker's voice, speed and articulation.
If MLV is used, each word is given at a similar level by watching the VU meter, and the mode is stated in the report.
In recorded material, a carrier phrase may come before each word; this phrase prepares the patient for the word.
The patient is told to repeat each word as heard, and to guess when unsure.
Responses are spoken; for patients who cannot speak, writing or picture pointing can be used.
In scoring, the word is judged as a whole; an error in even one sound makes the word wrong.
Some clinics also score at the phoneme level for extra information; the scoring type is then stated in the report.
Because the presentation level is high, masking of the opposite ear is often needed for the SDS, using speech noise.
Each ear is tested separately, and a different list is used for each ear.
Enough time is left between words for the patient to respond.
Sources use approximate categories to interpret scores; here we see one commonly used classification.
Ninety to one hundred percent is usually considered within normal limits.
Seventy five to eighty nine percent suggests slight difficulty, and sixty to seventy four percent moderate difficulty.
Fifty to fifty nine percent is interpreted as poor discrimination, and below fifty as very poor.
The limits vary by a few points between sources; these categories are a rough guide, and list length affects the result.
A score should always be interpreted together with the degree of hearing loss.
A word list is a small sample of a person's ability to discriminate speech.
The shorter the list, the greater the random variability of the score; it is larger with a twenty-five-word list.
Whether the difference between two scores is significant is judged with the critical difference tables of Thornton and Raffin.
For example, a small difference between two ears or two tests may not, by itself, mean a real change.
A score clearly lower than expected for the degree of hearing loss, however, needs special attention.
A disproportionately low score, especially in one ear only, is a finding to pass on to the physician for further assessment.
The word recognition score helps with counselling about the expected benefit from hearing aids.
A patient with a good score usually understands speech well when sounds are made loud enough.
Scores disproportionately low for the degree of loss add to the test battery, because they may suggest a problem beyond the cochlea.
Comparing aided and unaided scores in sound field can show how much the device helps speech understanding.
It is also used to monitor changes in the same patient over time.
But a score obtained in quiet does not fully reflect performance in noise; speech-in-noise tests exist for that.
Choosing a low presentation level makes the score look worse than it is, especially in sloping losses.
Forgetting to mask the opposite ear at a high presentation level can make the poorer ear's score look better than it is.
Using the same list again with the same patient after a short interval can lead to the words being remembered.
Reading words quickly or with exaggeration in live voice makes the score dependent on the speaker.
Responses are listened to carefully so that regional pronunciation differences are not counted as errors.

sahneler.metin: Do not write the score alone: also record the presentation level, list length, recorded or live voice, and the masking level.
cumleler: Here is a tip that is very useful when writing reports.
Do not write the word recognition score as a percentage on its own.
Add the presentation level, the list length, whether recorded or live voice was used, and the masking level.
Without this information, the same patient's score on the next test cannot be compared correctly.
The SDS is the percentage of words repeated correctly at a comfortably audible level.
The test usually uses phonetically balanced lists of monosyllabic words.
The presentation level is often thirty to forty decibels above the SRT, or the MCL; sloping losses may need a higher level.
Recorded material gives more standardized and comparable results than live voice.

sahneler.soru: 20 of 25 words correct. What is the score?
sahneler.aciklama: In a 25-word list each word is worth _4 percent_: 20 times 4 is 80.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in a twenty-five-word list, the patient repeated twenty words correctly. What is the score in percent?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: eighty percent.
In a twenty-five-word list each word is worth four percent; twenty times four is eighty.
